lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- Numbers, Data and Results: Saying What You Found
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Dejair Caitano do Nascimento | Lesson 9 -- Numbers, Data and Results
lesson.grammar_point: quantifiers with countable and uncountable nouns

listenings.text: A short warning before you present your numbers this week. In English, the word significant does not mean big. It means the difference is probably not chance. So a very small difference can be significant, and a very large difference in twelve patients may not be. Please do not say significant when you mean important, because half the room will hear a statistical claim you did not intend to make. If you mean it matters to the patient, say it matters to the patient. And one more thing. When you have few patients, say so early and say it yourself. If the audience finds it, it becomes a weakness. If you say it first, it becomes honesty.

Our sample was small. Sixty patients, and I will say that at the beginning so nobody has to ask. We do not have much data on the first three months, because the pain diaries came back incomplete, and that is a real limitation. What we do have is two years of follow-up on forty-one of them. Pain scores decreased in most of that group, and increased in a few, and the difference is significant. But I would rather say the treatment helps many patients than say it works, because we still do not know which patients, and that is the question I brought to this congress.
